title: The ladder of practice
hookLine: Krishna gives a path with a step for every kind of day
carry: if you can't, the next rung still reaches god

cards: The first week after an injury, a good physical therapist says: today, walk to the door and back. You can't. Fine.
Stand up and sit down five times. You can't do that either. Fine.
Squeeze this ball. Nobody leaves the room with nothing to do; there's always a smaller step that still counts. Chapter twelve has a stretch that works exactly like that.
Krishna has just named the goal. Then, instead of repeating it louder, he hands Arjuna smaller and smaller steps.

teach.b: Here's the ladder, verses eight through eleven, from the top. Fix your mind on me, let your understanding rest in me, and you will live in me. That's the whole goal in one sentence.
Verse nine: if you can't hold your mind steady on me, seek me through practice. The Sanskrit is abhyasa, coming back again and again. It first came up in chapter six, with the restless mind.

teach.h: IF YOU CAN'T, WORK AS OFFERING.
teach.b: Verse ten: if you can't even practice, make your work for my sake. Do your ordinary actions as an offering, and you'll reach perfection that way.

teach.h: IF YOU CAN'T, LET GO OF THE FRUIT.
teach.b: Verse eleven, the bottom rung: if you can't do even that, take refuge in me, keep yourself in check, and give up the fruit of all your actions. Four rungs, and each one below the top begins the same way: if you can't.
There's no scolding in it. No verse says you've failed. Each one says, then here's the next thing.
Then verse twelve turns the ladder around. Knowledge is better than practice. Meditation is better than knowledge.
And giving up the fruit of action is better than meditation, because peace follows that letting go right away. The lowest rung holds something the higher ones need.
Commentators read this verse in different ways and don't rank the steps alike. What the text does is plain: no one is left without a road to God.
It's why Hindus count so many things as real devotion: meditation, japa, work offered to God, letting go of the result.

how: Many Hindus read Gita 12.8–12.12 as permission to begin wherever they are: some meditate, some keep a daily practice like japa, and many simply offer their ordinary work and let go of the result.

o: practice: coming back again and again
a strict vow kept for a fixed time
deep study of the sacred texts

games.q: the rungs of the ladder — tap the pairs.
p: if you can't, work for my sake
if you can't, give up the fruit

s: in chapter 12, the lower rungs are scolded as failures
each rung below the top starts 'if you can't' and simply offers the next step. no verse scolds.
verse 12 says giving up the fruit is better than meditation
it says peace follows that letting go right away.
abhyasa means practice: coming back again and again
the same word the Gita used for the restless mind in chapter six.

games.q: you're Arjuna. you've heard 'fix your mind on me' and you know you can't hold it. what does Krishna say next?
o: then you're not ready for this path.
games.why: then practice. each lower rung begins with 'if you can't', and none of them sends anyone away.

practice: Rest your attention on whatever you hold most dear, a name, a face, or just stillness, and when it slips, as it will, drop one rung: come back to the breath, again and again.
If even that feels like too much today, quietly dedicate one thing you'll do later, and if you can't manage that, simply let go of how today will turn out. Any rung counts.

wordCard.voice: Abhyasa, practice, the coming back again and again. Gita twelve, eight to twelve: fix your mind on the divine; if you can't, practice; if you can't, work as offering; if you can't, let go of the fruit.

orig.note: Sanskrit: abhyasa, practice, repeated effort; the rung below 'fix your mind on me' in Gita 12.9.

carryVoice: Your line: if you can't, the next rung still reaches God. Abhyasa means coming back, again and again. That's day two hundred two.
